base: Background. Cross-platform transcriptomic harmonization benchmarks rely on individual success metric each: correlation with a reference profile, classifier accuracy, or a composite imported from single-cell integration. We found no published study that computes multiple orthogonal metric classes over one set of harmonization approaches and measures overlapping between the best approaches by these metrics.

base: Methods. We used the 2,234 approaches of the recent real-world benchmark: 31 harmonization methods, 14 batch-removal strategies, 3 imputations and 2 post-removal settings on 7,174 B-cell lymphoma transcriptomes. We assigned its 87 polarity-adjusted metrics to five classes (global, local, distributional, structural, and the composite group which is a mean of all the previous metrics) and added three biology-facing classes: within-cohort marker correlation (L), cross-batch rank agreement of a marker panel (M), and leave-one-batch-out (LOBO) prediction of diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, follicular lymphoma and normal B cells (N). Each class resulted in top 112 approaches (5%) by its own rank-percentile composite, and we measured overlap by the Jaccard index.

base: Results. Harmonization methods of high harshness such as quantile normalization matched different batches to the same shape of distribution but were inferior by local and global metrics. Local and composite metrics resulted in the largest overlap of best approaches (0.333, 56 shared). Classes L and M, M and N - shared no approach, whereas L and N shared one approach. The 15 approaches selected by the published clustermap shared none of the 112 that class N elected. Class N resulted in the ComBat family in 84 of its 112 places and class M elected two methods whose median marker correlation was -0.0007 and -0.0082. Of the 32,746 three-class LOBO folds, 15,436 (47.1%) carried one class and reached a median macro F1 of 0.903, against 0.7334 on the rest.

base: Conclusions. Best transcriptomic harmonization approach is highly contingent on the quality metrics used. We provide a six-step recipe for metric classes, their thresholds and the cross-batch tests for the robust selection of best approaches.

base: The harmonization quality criteria are especially important in datasets where the biological contrast is small compared to the batch level technical differences. In the case of germinal center (GC) B-cell lymphomas, expression profiling splits diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) into germinal-centre and activated B-cell types ⟦CIT:(Alizadeh et al. 2000)⟧ predicting survival after chemotherapy ⟦CIT:(Rosenwald et al. 2002)⟧. Survival in follicular lymphoma (FL) is predicted by subtle differences in immune-cell signatures of the microenvironment ⟦CIT:(Dave et al. 2004)⟧, and a 23-gene score separates FL patients into two outcome groups under immunochemotherapy ⟦CIT:(Huet et al. 2018)⟧. These small-scale transcriptomic differences are challenging to survive transfer between materials and platforms, explaining the cell-of-origin assignment reinvention for formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue ⟦CIT:(Scott et al. 2014)⟧ and multiple cohort sources for genetic subtypes of DLBCL ⟦CIT:(Chapuy et al. 2018; Schmitz et al. 2018)⟧. The same transfer problem governs expression signatures outside lymphoma, for example microsatellite instability status ⟦CIT:(Sorokin et al. 2021)⟧, therapy prescription in colorectal ⟦CIT:(Sorokin et al. 2022)⟧ and kidney cancer ⟦CIT:(Gudkov et al. 2022)⟧ and DNA repair pathway activation in thyroid tumors ⟦CIT:(Vladimirova et al. 2021)⟧. In a recent T-cell lymphoma xenograft study, principal-component analysis (PCA) showed only a partial overlap between primary tumors and their matched xenografts, which the authors attributed to tumor content and host cells, and that variation was removed by surrogate variable analysis (SVA) ⟦CIT:(Fiore et al. 2025)⟧.

Class L placed 93 of its 112 best approaches under the unharmonized output 01_raw and the minimally changed 36_explobatch, so it rewarded the approaches that change expression least. Batch PCReg separated methods more strongly than batch-removal strategies (Kruskal-Wallis effect size ε² = 0.739 against 0.100), with the RNA-seq-only strategy highest on batch PCReg and the FFPE-only strategy least often passing the joint class L and M quality gate. Local and composite metrics resulted in the largest overlap (Jaccard index 0.464, 71 shared approaches). Classes L and M, M and N - shared no approach, whereas L and N shared one approach, the unharmonized output 01_raw under the rare-batches-removed strategy with softimpute imputation and post-removal. The 15 approaches selected by the published clustermap shared none of the 112 that class N elected. Class N resulted in the ComBat family (05_combat, 29_combat_ref, 06_combat_seq and 08_inmoose_combatseq) in 84 of its 112 places. base: A harmonization approach is defined as one combination of batch-removal strategy, imputation, harmonization method and post-removal. We defined the approaches set by the condition that fewer than 5% of samples carry no defined expression value for all genes (pct_samples_allNA < 5). This set contained 2,234 approaches over 31 methods, 14 strategies, 3 imputations and both post-removal settings. Two methods, 34_arsyn and 38_harman, had a minimum of 74.23% of samples with no defined expression across all 84 of their approaches and were not included into the final approach set. Shambhala-2 was implemented using its standard P0 and Q0 calibration datasets and was named as 20_shambhala in the benchmark.

base: We assigned each of the 87 polarity-adjusted scoring metrics of the source benchmark ⟦CIT:(Nikitin et al. 2026 Sep 17)⟧  to one of four classes: global, covering principal component regression (PCReg), the dispersion separability criterion (DSC), per-component R2 and the variance explained by each principal component; local, covering the k-nearest-neighbour batch-effect test (kBET), the integration and cell-type local inverse Simpson’s indices (iLISI and cLISI), average silhouette width and graph connectivity; distributional, covering the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistics and per-gene batch quantities; and structural, covering tSNE and UMAP embedding statistics, intra- and inter-group distances, the distance ratio and the Watermelon score (Supplementary File X). A fifth class, the composite, is the equally weighted mean of those four classes.
new: Of the 344 quality metrics registered by the source benchmark (Supplementary File 2 of the source benchmark), 87 carry a scoring polarity and are used for every ranking below, and the remaining 257 are descriptive. Of the 87 scoring metrics, 51 have positive and 36 negative polarity, meaning that a higher or a lower value, respectively, is better. We assigned the scoring metrics of the source benchmark ⟦CIT:(Nikitin et al. 2026 Sep 17)⟧ to four classes by their column prefix: global, covering the 11 metrics of principal component regression (PCReg) and the dispersion separability criterion (DSC); local, covering the KNN batch-effect test (kBET), the integration and cell-type local inverse Simpson’s indices (iLISI and cLISI), average silhouette width, the cell-specific mixing score and graph connectivity; distributional, covering the Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) statistics and the per-gene coefficient of variation of batch means; and structural, covering tSNE and UMAP embedding entropy and centroid dispersion, the distance ratio and the Watermelon score (Supplementary File 1, sheet Metric_class_assignment). The per-component R² and variance-explained columns carry no polarity, so they are descriptive and enter no class, and the seven scoring metrics that describe missing values and bimodality are likewise left unassigned. A fifth class, the composite, is the equally weighted mean of those four classes.

base: Class N metrics were designed as leave-one-batch-out prediction to measure a transferability and generatability of the best harmonization approaches selected. For each approach and each of the 24 RNA batches we excluded this batch and fitted logistic regression in principal components on the training batches alone for the three-class target (DLBCL, FL and normal B cells) and for the two-class target (FL against DLBCL). Then we projected the PCA coordinates at the held-out batch and predicted its biology labels using the previously fitted logistic regression, calculating Area Under Curve (AUC) and F1 scores. We also controlled this calculation using 100 biological label permutations and averaged all the N class metrics separately on multiclass batches (having more than one biology class) and on all batches. Multiclass-only batches were selected in order to remove a potential F1/AUC bias in batches that contain single biology group.

For each approach and each of the 24 RNA batches we excluded this batch and fitted logistic regression in principal components on the training batches alone for the three-class target (DLBCL, FL and normal B cells) and for the two-class target (FL against DLBCL). Then we projected the PCA coordinates at the held-out batch and predicted its biology labels using the previously fitted logistic regression, calculating Area Under Curve (AUC) and F1 scores. We also controlled this calculation using 100 biological label permutations and averaged all the N class metrics separately on multiclass batches (having more than one biology class) and on all batches. Multiclass-only batches were selected in order to remove a potential F1/AUC bias in batches that contain single biology group. The AUC is undefined on a held-out batch with a single biology group, so every AUC mean is a mean over multiclass batches only.

base: Group comparisons across three or more groups used the Kruskal-Wallis H test, and monotone associations used the Spearman correlation coefficient. Per-strategy coefficients were analyzed as their ranges and medians and selected groups were reported by their medians and median absolute deviations (MAD). We ran the analyses under Python 3.11 with pandas 2.3.3, numpy 1.26.4, scipy 1.12.0, scikit-learn 1.3.2, statsmodels 0.14.1, matplotlib 3.10.8 and seaborn 0.13.2.
new: Group comparisons across three or more groups used the Kruskal-Wallis H test, with ε² as its effect size, and monotone associations used the Spearman correlation coefficient. Two groups were compared by the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, and matched pairs of approaches, which share strategy, method and the remaining pipeline settings and differ in one factor only, by the two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Proportions were compared between two groups by the two-sided Fisher's exact test and against their distribution in the analysis set by the chi-square goodness-of-fit test or the two-sided binomial test. The number of strategies in which one harshness tier ranked first was compared with the one-in-three chance level by the two-sided binomial test, and a count of strategies with a lower value on one principal component than on the next by the two-sided binomial sign test. The overlap of two elected sets was compared with the overlap expected for two random sets of the same sizes by the hypergeometric distribution, reported as the probability of an overlap at least as large, or at least as small, as observed. All p-values are raw, without correction for multiple testing. Per-strategy coefficients were analyzed as their ranges and medians and selected groups were reported by their medians and median absolute deviations (MAD); the spread of group means is reported as their range, the maximum minus the minimum. We ran the analyses under Python 3.11 with pandas 2.3.3, numpy 1.26.4, scipy 1.17.1, scikit-learn 1.8.0, statsmodels 0.14.6, matplotlib 3.10.8 and seaborn 0.13.2.

base: The remaining global metrics closely reproduced PCReg and added little separation. DSC for the batch column followed PCReg along a monotone sigmoid (Supplementary Figure 3C), and DSC for the platform column followed DSC for the batch column linearly on a logarithmic scale (Supplementary Figure 3D). All 15 clustermap approaches were below the overall median batch DSC of 0.962, although the four MNN approaches (0.781 to 0.957) located at the boundary, about two orders of magnitude higher than the FSQN R approaches (0.0013 to 0.0098). Such behavior can be explained by the definition of DSC as between-group scatter divided by within-group scatter, which is sensitive to outliers. Average silhouette width tracked PCReg in a noisy manner, with the Affymetrix-only and FFPE-only strategies worst (means of 0.165 and 0.078, against a range of -0.066 to -0.019 elsewhere, Supplementary Figure 3I) and 02_median_scaling and 33_amdbnorm best (-0.286 and -0.276, Supplementary Figure 3J).
new: The remaining global metrics closely reproduced PCReg and added little separation. We first compared PCReg for the batch column with PCReg for the coarser platform and cohort columns (Supplementary Figure 3A, B). Because one platform can correspond to two or three batches, PCReg by platform followed PCReg by batch almost linearly (Spearman ρ = 0.974, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰, Supplementary Figure 3A), with the FFPE-only and FF-only strategies closest to the diagonal, where each platform keeps a single batch. PCReg by cohort followed PCReg by batch less closely (ρ = 0.606, p = 2.1 × 10⁻²²⁴), and most approaches retained more cohort-related than batch-related variance (Supplementary Figure 3B). DSC for the batch column followed PCReg along a monotone sigmoid (ρ = −0.970, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰, Supplementary Figure 3C). DSC for the platform column followed DSC for the batch column linearly on a logarithmic scale (ρ = 0.966, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰, Supplementary Figure 3D). DSC for the cohort column, in contrast, formed two clouds of points that the strategies did not explain and that more plausibly reflect the harmonization method (ρ = 0.544 against batch DSC, p = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁷², Supplementary Figure 3E). All 15 clustermap approaches were below the overall median batch DSC of 0.962 and lower than the remaining approaches (Mann-Whitney p = 0.011). The four MNN approaches of the group lay at the boundary (0.781 to 0.957). The FSQN R approaches lay about two orders of magnitude lower (0.001 to 0.010). Such behavior can be explained by the definition of DSC as between-group scatter divided by within-group scatter, which is sensitive to outliers. The tSNE centroid dispersion by batch decreased with batch PCReg along an arc (ρ = −0.864, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰, Supplementary Figure 3F, G). A subgroup of 11_harmony approaches under the FF-only and FFPE-only strategies lay below this trend, although their dispersion did not differ from that of the other methods within either strategy (Mann–Whitney p = 0.32 and 0.15, respectively). Linking each approach with and without post-removal showed that post-removal raised batch PCReg under every one of the 14 strategies (Wilcoxon signed-rank, p ≤ 4.3 × 10⁻⁶ for each; Supplementary Figure 3H). The shift was largest in the Affymetrix-only strategy, with a median of 0.075 against 0.007 to 0.028 elsewhere, presumably because post-removal drops the already quantile-normalized SOM cohort, which makes up a large share of this strategy. Average silhouette width tracked PCReg in a noisier manner (ρ = −0.630, p = 1.9 × 10⁻²⁴⁷, Supplementary Figure 3I, J). The Affymetrix-only and FFPE-only strategies were worst, with means of 0.165 and 0.077, each above the other strategies (Mann-Whitney p ≤ 3.8 × 10⁻⁷, Supplementary Figure 3I). The best methods were 02_median_scaling and 33_amdbnorm, with means of −0.286 and −0.276 (p ≤ 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ against the rest, Supplementary Figure 3J).

base: We defined the PCReg metric so that 1 denotes the best possible overlap in PCA space for a given column, that is, none of the variance is explained by that column. Conversely, 0 PCReg means that the entire variance is explained by the column, and this is the worst scenario for batch columns (RNA_BATCH, PLATFORM_RNA, COHORT_LABEL, RNASEQ_SOURCE) and the best one for the biology one (Major_Group, Diagnosis_cell_type_unified, TUMOR_NORMAL). Because the variance is unevenly distributed across the PCs, we compared PCReg RNA_BATCH against R2 of RNA_BATCH in the first PCs by harmonization methods and batch removal strategies (Supplementary Figure 2D, 2E, respectively). As expected, we observed a strong negative relationship between the two, with the clustermap best approaches occupying the lower right corner of the plot. 10_mnn, 20_shambhala and 16_fsqn_r were shifted above the main diagonal, suggesting that their batch-explained variance is moved towards lower rank PCs. The same was true for the C strategy (Supplementary Figure 2E).

base: We separately investigated distribution of batch-associated variance over principal components by batch removal strategies. Ten of the 14 strategies, and 19 of the 31 methods, placed a lower batch-explained R2 on the first principal component than on some later one (Figure 1C, Supplementary Figure 2F). Among the five methods whose explained variance decayed most slowly, four (excluding 20_shambhala) reached their maximum batch R2 away from the first component (Figure 1C). The clustermap group averaged 37.9% and 11.6% of total variance and 22.9% and 15.2% batch R2 on the first two components; 14_qsmooth, the weakest method on the PCA metrics, averaged 53.7% and 13.5% of variance with 90.8% and 67.1% batch R2; the unharmonized data averaged 73.5% and 9.7% of variance with 64.8% and 65.9% batch R2. The RNA-seq-only strategy and the clustermap group showed the lowest first-component variance (30.4% and 37.9%) among the batch removal strategies and the smoothest decay (Supplementary Figure 2F), whereas the Affymetrix-only strategy had the highest variance explained by the first component (66.0%). The individual principal components analysis therefore showed that harmonization benchmarking based on the first component only inherently underestimates batch effect, and harmonization methods can hide the batch-related variance into the lower rank principal components which should be accounted for during benchmarking.

We then visualized batch and biology LISI on heatmaps by harmonization method and batch removal strategy (Supplementary Figure 4C, D). The clustermap best approaches occupied local peaks of batch LISI (Supplementary Figure 4C) but not the corresponding local minima of biology LISI (Supplementary Figure 4D). Against the other approaches, the clustermap group had a higher batch LISI (Mann–Whitney p = 2.0 × 10⁻⁷). Its biology LISI was indistinguishable from theirs (p = 0.80), which reflects how small the biological differences are relative to the technical ones in this dataset. By strategy, the RNA-seq-only strategy had the highest batch kBET acceptance rate, followed by the two Affymetrix strategies and the FF-only strategy, whereas removing bad or rare batches, or keeping malignant samples only, left kBET near zero (Supplementary Figure 5D; Kruskal–Wallis across strategies p = 1.2 × 10⁻⁷⁸).

We also compared LISI with the embedding-based mixing metrics. The tSNE entropy of the batch labels followed batch LISI closely (Spearman ρ = 0.915, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰), and 10_mnn together with the three clustermap 04_sva approaches formed a separate linear trend with a higher entropy for a given LISI (Supplementary Figure 5E). By strategy the differences were smaller, and the no-removal, rare-batches-removed, Affymetrix-extended and microarray-only strategies lay on the lower side of the trend (Supplementary Figure 5F). tSNE centroid dispersion decreased as tSNE entropy rose (ρ = −0.493, p = 5.6 × 10⁻¹³⁷, Supplementary Figure 5G, H). 10_mnn, with a minority of the 04_sva, 11_harmony, 12_scanorama and 16_fsqn_r approaches, formed a diagonal cloud of high entropy, whereas the other methods formed two dense, round clouds (Supplementary Figure 5G). The strategies formed layers present in both clouds (Supplementary Figure 5H), so a given method can produce either good or poor batch overlap in the embedding, and the composition of the batches governs how well they mix locally. UMAP and tSNE entropy agreed almost exactly (ρ = 0.992, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰) and added no difference between methods or strategies (Supplementary Figure 5I, J). UMAP and tSNE centroid dispersion were also strongly related (ρ = 0.814, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰), with the same two clouds of methods (Supplementary Figure 5K) and each strategy present in both (Supplementary Figure 5L). The clustermap best approaches were spread along this trend line, so the selection gave priority to local mixing over group separation in both non-linear embeddings.

Finally, we compared LISI and kBET against PCReg (Supplementary Figure 6). Batch LISI rose with batch PCReg (Spearman ρ = 0.557, p = 1.4 × 10⁻¹⁸²), with 10_mnn, 04_sva, 11_harmony, 12_scanorama and 16_fsqn_r above the general trend (Supplementary Figure 6A). By strategy the approaches formed layers similar to, but noisier than, those of tSNE centroid dispersion against tSNE entropy (Supplementary Figure 6B). For the biology column the relationship was negative (ρ = −0.403, p = 4.0 × 10⁻⁸⁸), and the clustermap best approaches were spread uniformly over the plane (Supplementary Figure 6C). Strategies formed horizontal layers of variable PCReg and fixed biology LISI (Supplementary Figure 6D), the malignant-only and FFPE-only layers at the lowest LISI and the FF-only layer at the highest, in line with the number of biological classes each strategy keeps. kBET acceptance rate rose weakly with batch PCReg (ρ = 0.396, p = 1.1 × 10⁻⁸⁴, Supplementary Figure 6E), and only 04_sva and 10_mnn had a kBET above 0.1 in a sizable number of their approaches. By strategy, the RNA-seq-only approaches formed a compact group of high kBET and high PCReg (Supplementary Figure 6F), none of which was selected by the clustermap.

We then analyzed the Watermelon score, which measures how well an approach separates classes on a clustermap in gene expression space, by batch and by biology columns (Supplementary Figure 7G–J). On the batch column the clustermap group had a lower Watermelon score than the remaining approaches, a median of 0.318 against 0.352 (Mann-Whitney p = 5.0 × 10⁻⁴, Supplementary Figure 7G). On the biology column it did not differ from them (0.290 against 0.306, p = 0.086). The batch and biology scores were moderately related (Spearman ρ = 0.422, p = 5.0 × 10⁻⁹⁷, Supplementary Figure 7G). The lowest batch score belonged to 10_mnn and three RNA-seq-only 11_harmony approaches (Supplementary Figure 7G). By strategy, the Affymetrix-only strategy scored worst on the batch column, and the malignant-only and FFPE-only strategies, with four malignant classes each, scored best on the biology column (Supplementary Figure 7H). Averaged over all batch columns, the clustermap group again scored lower than the remaining approaches (median 0.311 against 0.368, p = 1.4 × 10⁻⁵, Supplementary Figure 7I). Averaged over the biology columns, the clustermap group did not differ from them (median 0.350 against 0.372, p = 0.21). The two averages were weakly related (ρ = 0.124, p = 3.6 × 10⁻⁹, Supplementary Figure 7I), 10_mnn formed a compact group of low batch scores (Supplementary Figure 7I), and the strategies separated into compact groups, the malignant-only approaches lowest on the biology average and the FFPE-only approaches highest, although both keep the same four malignant classes (Supplementary Figure 7J). new: We then compared the biology related metrics of classes L, M and N between the harshness groups and observed clear differences (Table 1; [FIG:sfig_harshness]A–L). Each metric was compared across the three tiers by the Kruskal-Wallis H test and between each pair of tiers by the two-sided Mann-Whitney U test, and the number of approaches behind each metric is given in Supplementary File 1, sheet Harshness_full. Low-harshness methods kept the within-cohort marker correlation close to its maximum ([FIG:sfig_harshness]A) and had the smallest marker-minus-housekeeping contrast ([FIG:sfig_harshness]B). A per-batch linear shift and scale leaves the order of samples within a cohort unchanged, and with it every within-cohort rank correlation, which explains why the low tier saturates class L. High-harshness methods lowered both the same-biology ([FIG:sfig_harshness]C) and the different-biology cross-batch agreement ([FIG:sfig_harshness]D), and they carried the smallest same-minus-different margin ([FIG:sfig_harshness]E) and the smallest margin gain over the unharmonized baseline ([FIG:sfig_harshness]F). Reshaping every sample onto a common distribution removes the rank structure shared by batches of the same biology together with the structure that distinguishes batches of different biology. On LOBO prediction the order reversed: the low tier had the lowest three-class macro F1 on all folds ([FIG:sfig_harshness]G) and on multiclass folds ([FIG:sfig_harshness]H), and the lowest two-class macro F1 on both cuts ([FIG:sfig_harshness]J, K), while the medium and high tiers were close to each other on the multiclass cut (Table 1). Methods that apply a per-batch monotone transform presumably keep, together with the within-cohort ranks, the batch structure that a classifier trained on the other batches never sees, so a held-out batch stays displaced from the training batches. Neither the three-class nor the two-class AUC separated the tiers ([FIG:sfig_harshness]I, L; Table 1). The permutation null lay far below every tier, with medians of 0.237 to 0.261 for the three-class F1 and 0.500 for both AUCs ([FIG:sfig_harshness]G, I, J, L).

base: Since none of the 87 scoring metrics in the published benchmark assess expression of biomarker genes, we deeply studied performance of L and M metric classes. These classes were visualized for the clustermap best approach in the benchmarking article but there were not extensively compared between batch removal strategies and harmonization methods. Plotting raw against harmonized expression, gene by gene and cohort by cohort, shows what each class is reacting to: the unharmonized baseline lies on the identity line by construction (Figure 4A), 13_fsmvn moves every point along a per-gene affine path and keeps the within-cohort order (Figure 4B), 12_scanorama returns a cloud with no relation to the input (Supplementary Figure 14A), and 29_combat_ref shifts the cohorts onto a common scale while keeping the within-cohort spread (Supplementary Figure 14B).

The four linear methods, 03_limma, 05_combat, 29_combat_ref and 13_fsmvn, moved every cohort along its own straight line, shifting and rescaling it, so the within-cohort order of the samples was kept exactly ([FIG:sfig_expression]A–D). Of the non-linear methods, 16_fsqn_r bent the cohort lines while keeping their order ([FIG:sfig_expression]E), and 17_quantile bent them and added scatter around the curve, which lowers the within-cohort rank correlation slightly ([FIG:sfig_expression]F). 10_mnn and 12_scanorama returned an almost constant value for each gene in every cohort, so the harmonized expression no longer followed the unharmonized one ([FIG:sfig_expression]G, H). Class L reads the within-cohort order, which every linear method keeps by construction, and class M reads the cross-batch rank structure, which a collapse onto a constant profile makes identical across batches.

base: Class L is saturated at the top of its range. Five methods returned a median within-cohort marker correlation of exactly 1.0000 (01_raw, 36_explobatch, 31_ruv3prps, 27_dwd, 21_harmonizr), and the low-harshness tier sat at 0.998. When class L elects on its own it therefore chooses unharmonized output. Of its 112 elected approaches, 55 are 01_raw and 38 are 36_explobatch, so 93 of 112 places go to output that is unchanged or close to unchanged, with 13_fsmvn and 02_median_scaling taking 7 each, 04_sva 4 and 03_limma 1 (Supplementary File 1, sheet Method_census_by_class). A marker correlation above 0.75 is therefore a gate that an approach must pass and cannot win on, and we treat it as such throughout.

base: Class M has the opposite failure. base: Class N asks whether a classifier fitted on the batches that are present can label the samples of a batch it has never seen. Across the analysis set this produced 32,746 three-class folds over 24 RNA batches. Of those, 15,436 (47.1%) contained a single biological class and reached a median macro F1 of 0.903, against 0.7334 over the 17,310 folds carrying two or more classes; inside the latter, two-class folds were the harder ones (median 0.629) and three-class folds the easier (median 0.804) (Figure 5C).
new: We then evaluated class N, which asks whether a classifier fitted on the batches that are present can label the samples of a batch it has never seen. Over the 2,234 approaches, leave-one-batch-out (LOBO) prediction of the three-class target produced 32,746 held-out folds over 24 RNA batches. Of these folds, 15,436 (47.1%) contained a single biological class. The other 17,310 folds carried two or three classes. Single-class folds reached a median macro F1 of 0.903, against 0.733 for these multiclass folds (Mann–Whitney U, p = 2.3 × 10⁻²²¹; [FIG:fig_prediction_n]C). Among the multiclass folds, two-class folds were harder than three-class folds (median 0.629 against 0.804, Mann–Whitney U, p < 10⁻³⁰⁰; [FIG:fig_prediction_n]C).

We then examined why a held-out batch with a single class scores higher. With one class present, the macro F1 of the fold reduces to the F1 of that class, so the fold tests whether the classifier assigns the diagnosis of the whole held-out cohort and does not test whether it separates diagnoses. The two fold types had close means (0.690 against 0.679) although their medians differed, which places the difference in the shape of the distribution. Single-class batches split into those labeled correctly in the median fold, such as several FF microarray batches at 1.000, and those that failed, such as the FFPE batches GPL887_FFPE_Unknown at 0.000 and GPL13938_FFPE_Unknown at 0.069 (Supplementary File 2, sheet Fold_composition). A mean over all folds therefore mixes the assignment of whole cohorts with the separation of diagnoses measured on the multiclass folds. For this reason we report every class N value on two cuts: the full cut, the mean over all held-out folds, and the multiclass-only cut, the mean over the folds that carry at least two classes.

We controlled every class N value with 100 permutations of the biological labels. Under permutation, the full-cut three-class macro F1 fell to tier medians between 0.237 and 0.261, against an observed median of 0.709 over all approaches ([FIG:sfig_harshness]G). The permuted two-class F1 fell to tier medians between 0.393 and 0.441 ([FIG:sfig_harshness]J). The median permutation p was 0.0099 in each tier, the smallest value that 100 permutations can give. The differences between methods in class N are therefore differences between classifiers that almost all predict above chance.

Taken together, cross-batch prediction elected a set dominated by the ComBat family, and the leading approaches kept that composition on both fold cuts and under the generalizability index. Nearly half of the held-out batches carry a single diagnosis, so a mean over all folds mixes the assignment of whole cohorts with the separation of diagnoses, and strategies that retain batches confounded with diagnosis reach the highest values. A benchmark that uses held-out prediction should therefore report the multiclass-only cut and the multiclass fold count beside every full-cut value, exclude the strategies that retain confounded batches before ranking, and compare the observed values with a label-permutation null.

base: This is the cost of choosing a criterion before running a benchmark. A study that reports global metrics would recommend 13_fsmvn, whose median full-cut LOBO F1 is 0.537 and whose median multiclass-only F1 is 0.624, both in the bottom five methods. A study that reports cross-batch rank agreement without the margin would recommend 10_mnn, whose median within-cohort marker correlation is -0.0007. A study that reports LOBO prediction alone would recommend ComBat-Seq implementations that return mean maximum expression values of 2.76 x 108 and 1.46 x 1011. Each recommendation is correct under its own criterion and fails under the next one. The choice of metric class therefore determines the recommendation more than the data do.

On the same cut, 03_limma was second to last of the 31 methods ([FIG:fig_prediction_n]A). Class M, read without the margin, would recommend 10_mnn and 12_scanorama, whose median marker correlations were −0.001 and −0.008. The other approaches had a median of 0.969 (Mann–Whitney U, p = 1.7 × 10⁻⁵⁰ for 10_mnn). Class N would recommend the ComBat family, whose count-based implementations 06_combat_seq and 08_inmoose_combatseq returned mean maximum expression values of 2.76 × 10⁸ and 1.46 × 10¹¹ (Figure 3E). Class L would recommend unharmonized or near-unharmonized output, 01_raw and 36_explobatch (Supplementary File 1, sheet Method_census_by_class). base: The practical consequence is that a benchmark has to state its metric classes, its gates and its held-out test before it ranks anything, and has to report all of them afterwards. Class L is a gate that an approach must pass and cannot win on, because a per-batch monotone transform scores near 1.0 by construction and the low-harshness tier sits at 0.998 while predicting worst of the three tiers (0.631 on the full cut). Class M has to be read as a margin against the unharmonized baseline at the same strategy and imputation, because agreement alone rewards collapse. Class N has to be cut by batch and reported on both fold cuts, because 47.1% of the held-out batches carry one class and score a median of 0.903 against 0.7334 for the rest, and because a confounded strategy reaches the highest value of all (0.958 full cut, 0.924 multiclass-only). We have drawn these three traps and the six steps around them as a recipe (Figure 6), in the same terms the analysis above used.
new:
Taken together, the four batch-facing classes and the composite agreed above chance in nine of their ten pairs, whereas the three biology-facing classes shared fewer approaches than chance with each other and elected sets built on different methods (Table 3). A benchmark that selects harmonization approaches should therefore declare its metric classes, its gates and its held-out test before ranking, and report the elected set of every class with the intersections and their chance expectation. Class L then serves as a gate, because a per-batch monotone transform keeps within-cohort marker ranks: the low-harshness tier holds a median marker correlation of 0.998 while predicting worst of the three tiers on the full cut (Table 1). Class M is read as the margin against the unharmonized baseline at the same strategy and imputation, because agreement alone rewards algorithms that make all profiles alike. Class N is reported on both fold cuts with the multiclass fold count, because 47.1% of the held-out batches carry one class, and with the bad-batch-retaining strategies excluded, because they reach the highest values of all (Table 2). Figure 6 draws these steps as a recipe.

base: We ran the same election eight times over one set of 2,234 harmonization approaches, changing only the metric class that was allowed to vote, and the winners changed with it. The largest agreement between any two elected sets of 112 approaches was 56 approaches (Jaccard 0.333), and that pair was a class and the composite built from it. Between the three biology-facing classes the agreement was one approach in total: marker preservation and cross-batch rank agreement shared none, cross-batch rank agreement and prediction shared none, and marker preservation and prediction shared one. The 15 approaches selected by a joint reading of 87 metrics shared none of the 112 that prediction elected.
new: We elected the top 5% of 2,234 harmonization approaches once for each of eight metric classes, changing only the class that ranked them, and compared the elected sets with the 15 approaches selected by the published clustermap. The largest overlap between two elected sets of 112 approaches was 71 shared approaches (Jaccard 0.464), between the local class and the composite that contains it (Table 3). The three biology-facing classes shared one approach in total, the unharmonized I_rare_batches_removed / softimpute / 01_raw / post1 elected by classes L and N, and each of their three pairwise overlaps was below the 5.6 approaches expected by chance. The clustermap selection shared no approach with classes L and N, which a set of 15 does by chance with probability 0.46. On the generalizability index its approaches ranked between 433rd and 2,022nd of 2,234.

base: Each class elected what it was built to reward. Marker preservation elected unharmonized and near-unharmonized output, because a per-batch monotone transform leaves within-cohort ranks unchanged and scores near 1.0 by construction. Cross-batch rank agreement elected the two methods that make all profiles alike, whose median within-cohort marker correlation is -0.0007 and -0.0082. Global variance metrics elected the two methods that drive batch PCReg to its ceiling, one of which ranks in the bottom five on prediction. Cross-batch prediction elected four implementations of ComBat, two of which return mean maximum expression values of 2.76 x 108 and 1.46 x 1011. Every one of these verdicts is defensible inside its own class and indefensible outside it.
new: Each class elected the approaches that maximize the quantity it measures. Marker preservation (class L) elected unharmonized and near-unharmonized output, because a per-batch monotone transform leaves within-cohort ranks unchanged. Cross-batch rank agreement (class M) elected 10_mnn and 12_scanorama, which make profiles alike and return median marker correlations of −0.001 and −0.008. The global class elected 03_limma and 13_fsmvn, two of the six methods that drive batch PCReg to saturation, and 13_fsmvn predicted held-out batches worse than the other methods (median full-cut F1 0.537 against 0.715, Mann–Whitney U, p = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁸). Cross-batch prediction (class N) elected four ComBat implementations, two of which, 06_combat_seq and 08_inmoose_combatseq, return mean maximum expression values of 2.76 × 10⁸ and 1.46 × 10¹¹ (Figure 3E).

base: Three properties of the metrics themselves caused most of that behaviour, and all three can be handled by reporting. A within-cohort correlation metric saturates, so it works as a gate at a stated threshold and does not order the approaches that pass: the low-harshness tier holds it at 0.998 while returning the lowest full-cut prediction F1 of the three tiers (0.631). An agreement metric rises whenever an algorithm converges profiles, so it has to be read as a margin between same-biology and different-biology pairs, taken against the unharmonized baseline at the same strategy and imputation; requiring both directions of that margin leaves 61 of 2,150 non-raw approaches (2.8%). A prediction metric depends on the composition of the held-out batch, so it has to be cut by batch and reported on both fold cuts: 15,436 of the 32,746 three-class folds carry one class and reach a median macro F1 of 0.903 against 0.7334 for the rest, and the highest prediction values anywhere come from a strategy that keeps the known-bad batches (full-cut F1 0.958, multiclass-only 0.924).

A prediction metric depends on the composition of the held-out batch, so it has to be cut by batch and reported on both fold cuts: 15,436 of the 32,746 three-class folds carry one class. These single-class folds reach a median macro F1 of 0.903 against 0.733 for the rest (Mann–Whitney U, p = 2.3 × 10⁻²²¹). base: We set these out as a recipe (Figure 6). Declare the metric classes before computing them. Compute every class over the full approach set instead of a shortlist. Use the within-cohort correlation as a gate at a stated threshold. Rank on a margin taken against an explicit unharmonized baseline. Validate with leave-one-batch-out prediction whose projection is fitted on training batches only, reported on both fold cuts with the multiclass fold count beside each value. Report the elected set of every class together with their intersections, so a reader can see which recommendation depends on which criterion. Applied to this dataset the recipe leaves a small set of approaches that pass every step, led by no removal with softimpute under 29_combat_ref, which reaches a full-cut F1 of 0.946, a multiclass-only mean of 0.887 over 11 multiclass folds and a marker correlation of 0.880.
new: We set these steps out as a recipe (Figure 6). First, declare the metric classes before computing them. Second, compute every class over the full approach set. Third, use the within-cohort marker correlation as a gate at a stated threshold. Fourth, rank on the class M margin taken against the unharmonized baseline at the same strategy and imputation. Fifth, validate by leave-one-batch-out prediction whose projection is fitted on the training batches only, reported on both fold cuts with the multiclass fold count beside each value. Sixth, report the elected set of every class together with their intersections, so that a reader can see which recommendation depends on which criterion. Applied to this dataset, 1,187 approaches pass the gate with a positive margin and carry at least five multiclass folds outside the bad-batch-retaining strategies. The leading one by full-cut F1 is no removal with softimpute under 29_combat_ref without post-removal (S0_no_removal / softimpute / 29_combat_ref / post0), with a full-cut F1 of 0.946 and a marker correlation of 0.880 (Table 2). Its multiclass-only mean was 0.887 over 11 multiclass folds.

base: The limits of this work follow from its design. All 2,234 approaches come from one dataset of germinal-centre B-cell lymphomas, so the numbers are specific to a setting in which the biological contrast is small and the technical contrast is large. The election threshold of 5% is a choice, and a different threshold changes the set sizes although not the ordering of the overlaps. Classes L and M rest on one 633-gene panel, and a different panel would move their members. The prediction class uses three diagnostic classes and 24 batches, so its folds are coarse. What does not depend on these choices is the finding that the classes disagree, because that disagreement is measured between sets drawn from the same 2,234 candidates by the same procedure.

The ordering of the overlaps did not depend on it, and all 36 pairs at each threshold are listed in Supplementary File 2, sheet Threshold_sensitivity. **Supplementary File 1. The analysis set, its metric classes and the statistical tests.** An Excel workbook with a README sheet and one sheet per table. Analysis_set: the 2,234 approaches, one row per approach, with the key columns, the flags used in the text and the metric values. Canonical_set_reconciliation: the reconciliation from the 2,407 completed approaches of the source benchmark [38] to 2,234. It includes the Shambhala identity check, which compares 20_shambhala and shambhala_P0std_Q0std over the 84 shared keys. The check finds 78 of 79 numeric columns identical, the exception being compute time. Metric_class_assignment: the 344 metrics of the registry, by the name they carry in Supplementary File 2 of the source benchmark (which holds their polarity, group and type), with a scoring and a metadata flag, their availability in the pinned snapshot and their Article 2 metric class. Class_percentile_scores: for each of the 2,234 approaches, the score of every metric class (the mean rank percentile of its metrics) and whether the class elected it. Generalizability_ranking: the 2,234 approaches ordered by the E1 generalizability index, with its six components. Method_census_by_class: the number of elected places that each harmonization method takes in each metric class. Strategy_and_imputation_summary: the metric medians grouped by batch removal strategy and imputation. Harshness_by_LMN: the Kruskal–Wallis tests of the class L, M and N metrics across the three harshness tiers. Harshness_full: the same test for every numeric class L, M and N column, 186 metrics, with the mean, median and median absolute deviation (MAD) and the number of approaches per tier and the pairwise Mann–Whitney p values. Paired_tests: the 285 hypothesis tests behind the comparisons in the text, each with its groups, group sizes, medians, statistic and raw p value. Scatter_correlations: the 97 Spearman correlations behind the scatterplot relationships, with n, ρ and p. Composite_dispersion: the contribution of each metric type and metric group to the composite score by strategy and by method, with the range and the standard deviation of the group means. PCA_component_means: the mean percentage of total variance and the mean RNA_BATCH R² on each of the first ten principal components, for every method, every strategy, the clustermap group and the unharmonized no-removal approaches.

**Supplementary File 2. Cross-batch structure, elected sets and prediction.** An Excel workbook with a README sheet and one sheet per table. Cross_election_matrix: the Jaccard index between the elected sets of every pair of the nine sets (eight metric classes and the 15 clustermap best approaches). Cross_election_pairs: the same 36 pairs with the set sizes, the number of shared approaches, the union, the Jaccard index, the overlap expected by chance and the hypergeometric p values for more and for less overlap than chance. Elected_sets_by_class: the approaches elected by each set. Agreement_specific_61: the 61 approaches that raise same-biology agreement and lower different-biology agreement against their unharmonized baseline, with their class L, M and N values. Margin_raw_and_delta: the class M columns of all 2,234 approaches, in raw form and with the unharmonized baseline subtracted. LOBO_summary: the class N metrics on both fold cuts and for both targets for the named groups of approaches and for the leading approaches. Per_batch_folds: the macro F1 and AUC of every held-out batch for the prediction best and the clustermap best approaches, for both targets. Fold_composition: for each held-out batch and number of biology classes, the number of folds and their median F1, AUC and sample count, pooled over approaches. Threshold_sensitivity: the overlap of every pair of elected sets when the election takes the top 2.5%, 5% or 10% of approaches, with the Jaccard index. It also gives the rank of each Jaccard index among the 36 pairs and the Spearman correlation of each threshold's Jaccard values with those at 5%.

**Supplementary File 3. The marker gene panel behind [FIG:sfig_marker_qc] and [FIG:sfig_gene_method].** An Excel workbook with a README sheet and four data sheets.
